newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Coffee again leads commodity pack, wheat off.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Coffee again leads commodity pack, wheat off.

text.p: The vigorous 1997 rally in the world price of coffee found renewed strength on Tuesday when New York's benchmark July futures contract for quality arabica beans hit a new contract high at $2.67 per pound.
This was up a strong 10 cents on the day and within striking distance of last week's 20-year high of $2.80 on the now expired-May contract.
Prices had headed lower at the outset after some weekend longs liquidated their positions on reports that Brazil, the biggest grower, had made it through the weekend without any damaging frost.

But buying soon developed in a sizzling world market where stocks are at the lowest for two decades and - until the winter in Brazil is over and the risk of frost has gone - there are fears about Latin American supply.
Elsewhere in commodity markets, activity was slow to gather pace after holidays on Monday in the United States and Britain.

But Chicago Board of Trade soft red winter wheat futures fell sharply in early trade and the September contract was quickly down more than half the 20-cent per bushel daily limit after rains fell in Kansas over the weekend, traders said.
The moisture improved crop prospects in dry areas of Kansas, typically the leading U.S. hard red winter wheat producing state, traders said.
Traders said Produce Grain and LIT each sold two million bushels July in early trade while Cargill Investor Services and ABN-AMRO Chicago Corp each sold one million July.
July wheat was soon down about 10 cents per bushel to around $3.67.
The benchmark Brent Blend of North Sea crude oil was sharply lower, down more than 80 cents around $19.25 per barrel after selling of light crude futures in New York, on weakness in gasoline prices.
Traders have been watching the gasoline market to provide direction with the approach of the summer "driving season," which traditionally begins with the Memorial Day holiday.
They did not seem to judge that supply was tight.
Precious metals were mostly steady with gold closing in London at $343.75 per ounce, up 70 cents on Friday.
Early interest came in palladium where a large borrowing order set prices jangling. Palladium quickly jumped about four dollars from its opening to $174.00/$175.00 an ounce.

Palladium had been firmer in Tokyo as dealers there began to see as overdone a bout of selling last week in reaction to news that delayed Russian exports to Japan, the biggest buyer, would begin for late May/early June.
U.S. and London markets were closed on Monday.Some key prices at 1745 GMT on Tuesday
